data.title: Cost of having a baby: Hospital bills are shockingly high in states you wouldn't expect
data.description:
(NEXSTAR) – It’s no secret raising a kid is expensive. Countless diapers, 18 years worth of food, childcare and, for some, the cost of college tuition. But before all that even starts, there’s one big bill many parents will be forced to pay: the hospital bill.

Even routine deliveries can cost families a shocking sum, depending on their insurance coverage. When things go wrong, the costs mount even higher.

The cost of having a baby in the U.S. is so high, it has become a subject of global fascination, with videos of people recounting their itemized bills going viral.

In one short video, a woman shows her bill on camera. The grand total was $45,000. “Thankfully my insurance covered the majority,” the voiceover says. She still apparently owed $1,982.93.

While that figure is a shock to anyone without a huge savings account, it’s not even abnormal. In fact, it’s below average, an analysis of medical bills by MoneyGeek found.

After analyzing claims data from 2021 to 2023, the personal finance site found the average out-of-pocket cost of a vaginal delivery was $2,563 and a C-section was $3,071. These estimated totals include the cost of staying at the hospital, the line item charges for medication, and seeing different types of physicians (obstetricians, anesthesiologists, etc.).

The states with the highest bills, surprisingly, are places often thought of having a low cost of living, like Nebraska, Oklahoma and South Dakota. Average deliveries in all three states can cost patients upwards of $2,500 out-of-pocket.

People with high-deductible insurance plans or complicated deliveries can end up paying as much as $5,000, the analysis stated.

Meanwhile, in Michigan, the average delivery costs $974 out-of-pocket. What accounts for such a big difference? In most cases, it comes down to what hospitals have negotiated with insurers, according to MoneyGeek.

As the California Health Care Foundation explains, differences in price between different hospitals has little to do with the quality of care received. It has more to do with how much competition there is in a market.

“Decades of research shows that prices for inpatient and outpatient services — from C-sections to CT head scans — are higher when there is less competition,” write Kristof Stremikis and Catherine Teare. “This happens when hospitals, medical groups, or health plans merge or buy their competitors. With fewer choices, a big system in one area can set higher prices and anti-competitive contract terms.”

Search the table below to see the average cost of having a baby in your state:

Note: The analysis only covered 45 states and Washington, D.C., with Alabama, Hawaii, North Dakota, Vermont and Wyoming not reporting enough provider data to be included. See the full dataset here.

Even if you’re one of the lucky ones with a sub-$1,000 hospital bill, you should probably stash away any extra savings. LendingTree estimates it costs about $303,418 to raise a child over 18 years.

data.title: The October term heralds another 'big year' for the Supreme Court
data.description:
October is when hype meets reality. In baseball, the final teams are sorted out for the playoffs, and your football teams are well into the winnowing-out process for the Super Bowl. For court nerds, the start of the October term at the Supreme Court can have a similar dynamic, as long-watched cases finally come up for oral argument. Although the court continues to accept cases on a rolling basis, this term is looking like another blockbuster, with cases that range from climate change to gun rights to parental rights.

The odds of making the oral argument docket make the NFL season look like a walk in the park. After thousands of petitions, the Supreme Court accepts on average between 70-80 cases for the coveted “writ of certiorari.” If you are a lower-court judge with an appealed case, this is one Super Bowl you would probably prefer to skip. The court generally reverses the cases it accepts for review. Last term, it had a 71 percent rejection rate, slightly up from the prior year.

This year already has a number of major cases that are likely to have transformative impacts on the law and society. Here are a few.

Climate Change

In Suncor Energy Inc. v. County Commissioners of Boulder County, Boulder sued energy companies under theories of public and private nuisance, trespass, unjust enrichment, and civil conspiracy, claiming that they knowingly contributed to climate change while misleading the public about its impacts.” The Colorado Supreme Court ruled for the city and the county in finding that such lawsuits are not barred by federal preemption. If the case is allowed to go forward, it would expose companies to potentially thousands of climate change lawsuits.

Gun Rights

October is already shaping up as a major Second Amendment term. Democratic cities and states have been banning the AR-15, the most popular rifle in the U.S., and the 9mm semi-automatic handgun, the most popular handgun in the U.S. These cases out of the Seventh Circuit in Chicago (Viramontes v. Cook County) and the Second Circuit in New York (Grant v. Higgins) will likely give long-awaited clarity on these bans. They could potentially close off a major circumvention of prior rulings to achieve sweeping gun control policies.

In addition to these cases, the court is considering the possible review of Calce v. New York. In that case, the Second Circuit upheld a stun gun ban. The court previously sent back a similar case out of Massachusetts after the First Circuit ignored prior rulings. The court stressed that the fact that a weapon did not exist at the time of the ratification of the Second Amendment (such as “electric arms”) does not mean that they fall outside of the constitutional protections. The addition of Calce would make this one of the most momentous Second Amendment terms in history.

Parochial Schools and Religious Discrimination

The court will return to another parochial school controversy this term. In prior cases, the court has repeatedly stepped in to prevent states from discriminating against religious schools in voucher or subsidy programs. In St. Mary Catholic Parish v. Roy, the Tenth Circuit upheld a Colorado provision that requires all preschools to agree not to discriminate on the “race, religious affiliation, sexual orientation, gender identity, income, or disability.” The Catholic challengers are arguing that the policy requires them to violate their religious values as a condition for participating in the preschool program and funding.

Parental Rights

In International Partners for Ethical Care, Inc. v. Ferguson, Washington amended its laws to delay shelters in notifying parents of a runaway child who has “gender-affirming treatment” — the standard used for children in abusive homes. Instead, the Department of Children, Youth, and Families is first notified. The Ninth Circuit rejected parental claims raised in the case due to a lack of standing.

The Right to a 12-Member Jury

In Kian v. Florida, chiropractor Hamed Kian was convicted of five counts related to practicing with a suspended license. Pursuant to Florida law, he was tried by a six-person jury. Kian argues that the law violated his Sixth Amendment right to a jury of 12 members.

Some of us are watching a few other cases. Not surprisingly, my two favorites deal with the freedom of speech. The court has yet to decide whether to accept D.A. v. Tri-County Area Schools in which the Sixth Circuit upheld a school ban on high school students wearing “Let’s Go Brandon” sweatshirts. In the view of many of us in the free-speech community, the case is a major potential First Amendment ruling in the making.

Some of us also hope that the court will take up Tiny Zaps v. Traxler, which deals with a ban on tattoos on the face, neck, or head as well as a ban on tattoo parlors within 1,000 feet of churches, school, or playgrounds. The South Carolina Supreme Court upheld the ban, and it could allow the court to reinforce free-speech protections for “body art.”

The late Justice Ruth Bader Ginsburg once said, “It’s hard not to have a big year at the Supreme Court.” That is certainly true, but this term is already pretty big, and the court still has plenty of slots to fill before January.

Jonathan Turley is a law professor who teaches a class on the Constitution and the Supreme Court and is the best-selling author of “Rage and the Republic: The Unfinished Story of the American Revolution.”

data.title: Trump rejects Iran's 7-day plan to end war, expects bombing to resume post-midterms: Report
data.description:
President Trump reportedly privately rejected Iran’s seven-day proposal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz and enter a ceasefire and is considering renewed military strikes against the country after the midterm elections in November.

According to a report from the Wall Street Journal citing U.S. officials, the president is skeptical over Iran’s ability to honor its end of the deal and told officials that he is contemplating resuming military strikes.

Under the proposal, Iran would reopen the strait and resume negotiations over its nuclear program.

Tehran is seeking several concessions from the U.S. in return, including an end to the U.S. naval blockade of Iranian ports, waivers on sanctions targeting Iranian oil sales and a ceasefire that would extend to Lebanon, according to the Associated Press.

Trump has not publicly responded to the proposal, but on Saturday morning, he reiterated his demand that Tehran not obtain a nuclear weapon and put an end to its uranium enrichment efforts.

“IRAN CAN NOT HAVE A NUCLEAR WEAPON!!!” Trump wrote on Truth Social.

Trump also posted an image Friday labeling the Strait of Hormuz, one of the world’s most important energy routes carrying roughly 20 percent of global oil supplies, the “Trump Strait.”

Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said Friday that the decision to reopen the Strait of Hormuz “now rests with the United States,” after Tehran offered a plan that it says could restore normal shipping through the critical waterway within a week.

“If the necessary conditions are met, the strait can be reopened, and normal maritime passage restored within seven days,” Araghchi told reporters on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly in New York. “The choice now rests with the United States.”

Araghchi said Iran conveyed a “concrete seven-day plan” to the U.S. through mediator Qatar following talks between the two countries this week.

“The seven-day timeline starts as soon as the United States accepts this plan,” he said. “If they accept this plan tomorrow, the seven days will start from tomorrow.”

Araghchi said the U.S. could carry out the steps required under the proposal within four or five days.

He argued that some were already included in commitments Washington made in a memorandum of understanding signed in June between the two countries that laid out plans for a temporary ceasefire, which later collapsed.

data.title: To make energy affordable again, end green mandates before the midterms
data.description:
Amid all the talk about affordability, the Environmental Protection Agency’s repeal of Biden-era climate regulations is set to save Americans $310 billion by restoring cheap baseload power.

The final rule eliminates the EPA’s 2024 Carbon Pollution Standards. Those standards exceeded the agency’s authority under the Clean Air Act by requiring emissions-control technologies that do not actually exist yet — or in the EPA’s words, have not been “adequately demonstrated.” Biden’s rules forced power plants to retire early by setting standards they could never meet.

The 2024 rule also failed to account for the recent Supreme Court decision in West Virginia v. EPA, which barred the EPA from misusing the act to manipulate Americans’ energy choices and drive electricity prices up.

“The Obama and Biden administrations implemented a war on coal to destroy reliable and affordable energy,” said EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin in a press statement. “The Trump administration has come in to protect American energy and to make sure you can afford to keep the lights on.” He said lower energy prices were “just the beginning.” 

“Realizing the full potential of American energy means more jobs, lower prices, and a more prosperous America.”

Democrats spent the summer talking a big game on “affordability,” but their energy approach raises prices across the board. Republicans should highlight that while the administration rolls back costly federal energy mandates that deep blue jurisdictions, such as Washington D.C., are imposing.

In the case of D.C., the energy mandate is so expensive that the city government exempted itself from following it. The District’s statue states that its new standard “shall not apply to electricity sold to the District of Columbia government, not including independent agencies, authorities, or instrumentalities.”

That hypocrisy needs more political attention. It creates a unique opportunity for President Trump and congressional Republicans to get a political win before the midterm. They can use constitutional authority to review D.C. Council legislation under the Home Rule Act to repeal these onerous mandates. The Constitution explicitly gives Congress “exclusive Legislation” over the District of Columbia, making this easy to do politically.

As a result of these so-called green mandates, D.C. electricity costs rose 66 percent — more than neighboring Maryland (50 percent) and Virginia (20 percent). The District’s renewable energy mandates have quadrupled compliance costs, from $65 million in 2020 to $272.6 million in 2025, for an average added annual burden of $775 per customer.

Why should every American pay a price that D.C.’s own government refuses to pay? 

Energy prices are a function of public policy more than anything else. Examining the costs of energy throughout the country, it becomes easier to put a finger on who’s responsible for high prices: Blue states pay far more than red states do. According to the Institute for Energy Research’s 2025 Always on Energy Research report, U.S. electricity prices spiked 27 percent under the Biden administration, with the vast majority of this price increase affecting blue states.

Aggressive green energy targets, primarily in Democratic-leaning jurisdictions, caused power bills to soar in areas like the District, New Jersey, Maryland, Virginia, Illinois, Delaware and Michigan, according to a recent study by the nation’s largest power grid operator. At the same time, states like North Carolina, Pennsylvania, Ohio, Kentucky, Tennessee, Indiana and West Virginia see no predicted price hike because they haven’t imposed green energy standards. 

These mandates have already cost mostly blue state residents $17.8 billion in compliance costs over the last decade, with this number expected to significantly increase as more regulations come online. The average New Jerseyans spend 19.8 cents per kilowatt-hour of electricity, almost twice what the average West Virginian pays. 

Those prices flatly contradict the “affordability” message that Democrats are running on. Republicans should highlight this massive discontinuity. If Washington wants to deliver on affordability, it can start by repealing energy mandates that are driving up electricity prices and making Americans pay more to keep the lights on.

Andrew Follett conducts research analysis for a nonprofit in the Washington, D.C. area.

data.title: Live updates: Trump attends Texas-Tennessee football game in Knoxville; US, China to cut tariffs on $30 billion worth of goods
data.description:
President Trump will attend the University of Texas vs. University of Tennessee football game in Knoxville at noon on Saturday — an appearance coming ahead of senators’ last chance to pass the Protect College Sports Act before recessing into a lame-duck period.

Trump will fly to Knoxville Saturday morning to watch the Texas Longhorns, ranked number one in the AP Top 25, face off against the Tennessee Volunteers, ranked 14th.

He is not expected to make any appearances on sports networks covering the game, as his fellow Republican, Sen. Ted Cruz (Texas), did earlier this month — appearing on ESPN’s College Gameday to tout legislation.

It is not yet clear whether television news broadcasters will cover Trump’s travels to and from the game, as the president barred CNN from reporters on Air Force One and taking its turn as the trips designated pooler — a rotating group of journalists who cover the president when space is limited, sharing their information with other networks. 

The White House has not yet named a replacement for CNN, who — along with MS NOW and Politico — have been locked in a legal battle with Trump after he attempted to ban them from his official residence.

Meanwhile, the Senate is preparing for its final week in session before a long recess will extend beyond election day in November. While some GOP candidates attempt to distance themselves from Trump’s policies after his approval rating hit a record low, Republicans in the Senate are preparing to make haste in passing legislation while they still hold a majority.

Following Chinese President Xi Jinping’s visit to Washington, D.C., it was announced that the U.S. and China agreed to cut tariffs on $30 billion worth of tariffs imported by one another, set up a channel for AI-related incidents and strengthen military crisis communications.

The move comes after Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent announced Wednesday that Washington and Beijing would extend their broader trade truce by two months, from Nov. 10 to Jan. 10, for a larger negotiation window.

data.title: US, China agree to cut tariffs on $30 billion worth of goods, set up channel for AI incidents
data.description:
The U.S. and China agreed to lower tariffs on $30 billion worth of goods each country imports from the other and launch new talks on artificial intelligence (AI) following President Trump’s summit with Chinese President Xi Jinping.

The agreements were part of an eight-point consensus reached during Xi’s three-day state visit to Washington, D.C., which ended Friday.

Under the trade agreement, the two countries will reduce tariffs on products considered “noncritical,” including agricultural and energy-related goods.

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said earlier this week that he and U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer had been in New York discussing lowering those tariffs to “most favored nation levels.”

The proposal was first floated during Trump’s May summit with Xi in Beijing and was still under negotiation in the days leading up to this week’s meetings.

The move comes after Bessent’s announcement Wednesday that Washington and Beijing would extend their broader trade truce by two months, from Nov. 10 to Jan. 10, giving officials more time to negotiate.

The U.S. and China also agreed to establish a channel for handling AI-related incidents and hold talks on the rapidly developing technology’s risks and benefits. The first AI-specific talk is scheduled for November.

Trump responded to rising pressure to address AI concerns and demands to impose safeguards by creating an “AI Force,” despite labeling the broader concerns a “hoax.” He also said he would be naming an “AI czar,” but ruled out Bessent from consideration amid speculation that he may be appointed to the role. 

Trump had signaled ahead of his talks with Xi that AI — which he has referred to as “super intelligence” — would be a major topic during the summit.

The final part of the U.S.-China agreement was to strengthen military crisis communications. The two countries planned to sign a memorandum of understanding aimed at preventing confrontations between their armed forces.

Xi returned to Beijing on Saturday, according to Chinese state media.

data.title: The future is here: What will a Millennial-Gen Z majority mean for America?
data.description:
Everyone knows millennials and Gen Z as the young, internet-native faces of American society. But the stereotype of millennials as the part-time barista working at the local coffee shop is out of date: Millennials are now 30 to 45 years old, and the oldest Gen Zers are turning 30. These Americans are far more likely to be your knee surgeon today than they are your barista. 

For decades, American politics has run on a binary that Baby Boomers built growing up amid the Cold War: communism versus capitalism, Team Red versus Team Blue. That framework fit a world with two clear sides. It fits a lot less neatly in 2026, when the free market and the internet age have handed us more choice than ever, from streaming platforms to ketchup brands. 

Except when it comes to politics. 

If there’s anything we should know about millennials and Gen Z, it is that they hate being neatly fit into a box. This explains why people nowadays display significantly less brand loyalty than before when looking at consumer habits and trends. And this also explains why millennials and Gen Z identify as political independents at far higher rates than older Americans. 

Data conducted by Gallup in January discovered that the majority of both Gen Z (56 percent) and millennials (54 percent) identify as political independents. This trend is likely to continue. Millennials and Gen Z combined already make up the largest voting bloc of the U.S. electorate. By 2028, Gen Z and millennials are projected to make up more than half of the electorate, and they will continue to dominate American politics for the next 20 years. 

This demographic has experienced nothing but political gridlock, a failing immigration system and a national debt that continues to spiral out of control. Put simply, these voters have seen nothing but ineffective governance in Washington and are ready for something different.

This year’s election marks the first time where we’re seeing serious, viable independent candidates emerge to meet this growing demand driven by younger voters. In fact, this year is seeing one of the largest surges of independent candidates in recent memory, with dozens of candidates vying for public office across the country.

They offer genuine, nonpartisan, commonsense solutions that these voters are yearning for. 

Millennials and Gen Z are not the future of American politics. They are the present. And this also means that independents are now a major, indisputable force that decides elections and shapes policy. From comprehensive immigration policy that secures our borders to AI/tech guardrails for children, there’s real potential for meaningful change that this demographic shift can usher in.

On immigration, younger voters reject the false choice between a wall and blanket amnesty; they want enforcement that actually works paired with legal pathways that exist, not a standoff that’s been stuck in place for 30 years. On AI and kids’ online safety, they’re equally unimpressed by regulate-everything and regulate-nothing. Having grown up as the first generations raised inside these platforms, they want guardrails that protect children without strangling the innovation that built the tools they use every day.

We should be encouraged that these generations are already thinking about one of the biggest of problems facing our country: Social Security insolvency. Writing for Fortune in August, Nick Lichtenberg noted that baby boomers are collecting 265 percent of what they paid into Social Security while millennials pick up the tab. Sixty-nine percent of Gen Z and 71 percent of millennials worry the program will run out before they ever see a dime.  

Neither party has offered a credible fix; both sides seem intent on kicking the can down the road. Independent millennials and Gen Z Americans know that this can is going to eventually hit a wall, and they’ll be left to pick up the mess. You already see Sens. Bernie Moreno (R-Ohio) and Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.) backing legislation to raise taxes instead of planning for lasting reform.

Millennials and Gen Z can back a solvency plan that is judged on whether it actually works for the generations footing the bill, not based on which party flinches first. 

Social Security’s looming insolvency is just one of these major policy areas where millennials and Gen Z will lead. And consider the possibilities that independents represent because they’re not bound by either party’s outdated ideologies. 

Remember, independents are not merely a trend driven by the historical unpopularity of the two parties. It’s a new era ushered in by the political maturation of the millennial and Gen Z generations.

The future is here, indeed.

Adam Brandon served as the president of FreedomWorks for more than a decade. Currently he is senior adviser at the Independent Center and author of “The Exhausted Majority: Building a Home for the Politically Homeless.”

data.title: Trump's polls sink further in warning sign for GOP
data.description:
President Trump’s approval ratings have sunk to new lows in several recent polls, driven by declining GOP support and souring views on the economy in a possible warning sign for Republicans just weeks out from the midterms.

In the latest Reuters/Ipsos poll, Trump’s overall approval fell three points from the previous week to an all-time low of 32 percent. Among Republicans, approval of his job performance dropped from 82 percent to 73 percent in a week, down from 86 percent in January 2026 and 91 percent just after his second inauguration.

“For really his entire political career, the president has enjoyed very strong support among the Republican Party and among his base, and that’s still true today, but it’s a bit less true,” Alec Tyson, senior vice president and lead pollster at Ipsos Public Affairs, told The Hill. 

Trump has seen a decline in his polling numbers since the Iran war started, according to Tyson, but the latest polling shows a clear dip in recent weeks, which the pollster said tracks with the “striking” drop in how Republicans view the president on economic issues.

Since January, Republicans’ approval of Trump’s handling of the economy has dropped 24 percentage points to 56 percent, while their approval of his handling of the cost of living has fallen 26 points to 44 percent.

“Those are striking numbers,” Tyson said. “Numbers that we hadn’t seen until recent weeks here in our Ipsos polling.”

A recent Quinnipiac poll similarly found Trump at his lowest approval to date on the economy, with only 32 percent approving his handling of the issue. Overall, 33 percent approved of his handling of his job, near the 32 percent record notched in July. 

The polls also point to a difficult national environment for Republicans ahead of November, though the outcome in Congress will depend on individual races.

In the Quinnipiac poll, voters favored Democrats by 11 points when asked which party they want to see control the House, 49 percent to 38 percent — a four-point shift from July, when Democrats led 48 percent to 41 percent.

Republican strategists differ on how candidates should respond, but some warn that dissatisfaction with Trump’s handling of the economy could depress turnout.

“There’s a major risk that a lot of Republicans will be staying home in November, while Democrats turn out in droves,” Republican strategist Bill F. B. O’Reilly told The Hill. 

“The dissatisfaction with the Iran war strategy and rising gas prices are sapping enthusiasm on the right at the worst possible time,” he added. “We have one month to turn that around.”

The latest NPR/PBS News/Marist Poll suggests Trump is weighing on voters’ choices for Congress, with only 30 percent saying the president is not much of a factor in their vote for Congress.

Anti-Trump sentiment also appears to be more motivating for registered voters, with 45 percent saying their congressional vote is mostly a vote against Trump, and 24 percent saying it’s mostly a vote for Trump.

Democrats held an advantage on several issues in the Marist poll. Voters trusted Democrats over Republicans to handle the economy, 42 percent to 34 percent, and to handle gas prices, 40 percent to 27 percent. The gap between the parties was tighter on immigration, though voters have grown more confident in the Democratic Party’s ability to handle the issue since 2024.

Tyson noted that Democrats also held a six-point advantage over Republicans on which party would better handle the economy in the latest Reuters/Ipsos poll. He called that “unusual” for an issue that has typically been among Republicans’ strongest.

He noted that Democrats’ improving numbers over the past year have “run in parallel with the president’s declining rating.” 

“Absolutely, that has implications for the midterms when folks are comparing the two parties or the candidates for the two parties, if the Democratic Party has opened up an advantage on the economy, in part due to the drag of the president’s performance for his own party on the issue,” Tyson said. 

Republican political analyst Ford O’Connell said GOP candidates need to counter those numbers by going on offense over the economy, and making the case that conditions have improved under Trump and will continue to do so if Republicans retain control of Congress.

He also pushed back on Democrats’ messaging on gas prices, saying they have “spent the last 15 years trying to kill oil and natural gas production, so the notion that they care about gas prices is nonsense.”

“Republicans have not made the case that when Trump came into office, the Biden economy was far worse than anyone imagined, and it was not going to be fixed overnight. That’s the problem: is they’re playing defense versus offense,” O’Connell told The Hill.

O’Connell cautioned against treating national polling as a prediction of the election outcome, noting some results have been inconsistent. He also doesn’t believe the public is sufficiently factoring in the effect of mid-decade redistricting pushes in several states.

“Republicans are definitely facing strong headwinds, but that does not mean that the game is over. And if they stop pushing right now, they will certainly lose both the House and the Senate,” he said. “And they should hold onto the Senate and could conceivably have a very narrow loss in the House, or, if something totally breaks their way, could actually hold the House by basically the status quo that they have now.” 

Alan Abramowitz, a political scientist at Emory University, said the generic congressional ballot is “usually a very good indicator” of the midterm landscape, along with the president’s approval rating, though he said there are other mitigating factors that can affect the outcome.

“In general, the president’s party tends to lose more seats when the president’s approval rating is underwater, when the president is unpopular,” Abramowitz said, adding, however, “It’s not a perfect relationship by any means.” 

He cited the strong economy under former President Clinton in 1998 and former President Bush’s high approval ratings after 9/11 in 2002 as factors that helped their parties in those midterms. Abramowitz pointed to the Supreme Court’s decision to overturn Roe v. Wade as a significant factor in 2022, when Republicans won the House but secured only a slim majority despite former President Biden’s low approval ratings. 

Tyson noted while the economy will likely matter more than Trump’s approval ratings in November, the two issues are closely related, especially if voters don’t see the president as responding to their concerns. The pollster said he sees the last four years as an era that could be “defined by the politics of household affordability.”

“These are the same concerns that powered the president to a popular-vote election two years ago,” Tyson said. “But now, two years later, these same frustrations that Americans have been having for some time are increasingly directed at the president and, to some extent the Republican Party.”

data.title: Trump faces growing GOP dissent in heartland as policies bite
data.description:
A growing number of Republicans in the heartland are breaking with President Trump on policies that are unpopular as the GOP worries about paying the price for them in the upcoming elections. 

Lawmakers and candidates in Iowa, Michigan and Ohio have called for a quick end to the Iran war amid high gas and diesel prices and the growing unpopularity of the war. 

Sen. Roger Marshall (R-Kan.) was critical of Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) operating in his state Wednesday, calling on the agency to better coordinate with local law enforcement. 

And Sen. Todd Young (R-Ind.) spoke out against Trump inviting Russian President Vladimir Putin to the Group of 20 (G20) summit this December in Miami.

The pushback comes as Republicans are worried about the party’s performance in the November midterm elections. 

“If Donald Trump isn’t popular in your district or state, you should expect your candidates to try to create some distance. That is the ordinary course of business,” one former Trump administration official told The Hill. 

“What is different right now is that Trump is unpopular in a lot more districts, and a lot more states, than anyone expected. But the die is pretty much cast. This is his party now. If it wins, it’s because of him. If it loses, it’s because of him. There’s just no two ways about that,” the former official continued. 

The Iran war has led to a number of Republicans facing tough reelection bids calling for a resolution to the conflict. 

Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) echoed those calls in an interview with a local television station Thursday, noting the U.S. military operation in the country accomplished what it needed to. The Speaker did not call for an immediate end to the war and did not provide any details on how the administration could end the conflict.

However, his remarks came after a number of vulnerable Republicans in the House and Senate called for an end to the conflict in an effort to bring prices down. 

“Clearly members are increasingly nervous about the costs of the war and that there seems to be no end in sight and still no definition of what success means,” said Doug Heye, a longtime Republican strategist. “No doubt we’ll hear more Republicans echoing similar concerns.”

“It’s the right move to make,” he said of Republicans distancing themselves, “but impossible to tell how much success it will have.”

The war has had a particularly acute impact on Midwestern Republicans as prices for gas and fertilizer skyrocketed as a result of the war. Midwestern and Southern states including Michigan, Wisconsin, Oklahoma, Ohio, Mississippi and Tennessee are on the list of states that have seen the biggest percentage increases in their gas prices from a year ago, according to GasBuddy.

Iowa Senate candidate Rep. Ashley Hinson (R-Iowa) and Wisconsin gubernatorial candidate Rep. Tom Tiffany (R-Wis.) both called for an end to the conflict earlier this week. Meanwhile, Iowa Reps. Zach Nunn (R) and Mariannette Miller-Meeks (R), who are each facing uphill reelection battles, voted earlier this month on a war powers resolution that would have curbed Trump’s authority in the conflict. 

Former Rep. Mike Rogers, the GOP’s Senate nominee in Michigan against progressive Democrat Abdul El-Sayed, also said in a recent campaign ad that “the war with Iran needs to end and end quickly.”

And Sen. Jon Husted (R-Ohio) told Politico earlier this week that “the war needs to come to an end as quickly as possible so that we can lower gas prices.”

He is facing a tight race against former Democratic Sen. Sherrod Brown.

“We’re at the tail end of September here. Farmers across the Great Plains, across the Midwest, they’re gearing up for harvest season. That is acres upon acres of products and goods that American farmers are going to be harvesting this fall,” said Preya Samsundar, a GOP strategist.

“They understand what the president is doing is important, but their constituencies are suffering,” she continued, referring to Trump’s objectives in Iran. “They’re not seeing immediate relief, the prices continue to rise and they have to give an account for that.” 

Affordability remains a top issue for voters across the board. 

A CNN/SSRS poll found that support for the war among self-identified Republicans dropped more than 10 percentage points since March, from 73 percent to 60 percent.

“I think it’s a conflation of things,” said Jason Cabel Roe, a Michigan-based GOP strategist, when asked why Midwestern Republicans have broken with Trump. “Particularly in Michigan, we also have the added economic pressures of the tariff war with Canada. That, I think, only exacerbates the affordability issue in Michigan.” 

In a statement to The Hill, the Republican National Committee said the party’s candidates are running the races necessary to best represent their districts. 

“Unlike the Democrats who are in a full-blown civil war with extremists, Republicans remain united behind the President’s agenda of cutting taxes, lowering drug costs, and securing our communities. We are laser focused on winning,” said Natalie Baldassarre, the committee’s national press secretary. 

Republicans have also been critical of Trump extending an invite to Putin to the G20 summit later this year to be held at Trump National Doral Miami in December.

Young said the visit from Putin would only be valuable if he came to announce concessions, according to The Wall Street Journal. 

“I think elevating Vladimir Putin is not where we should be focused right now,” he told reporters. “It should be trying to come up with ways to bring him to the table for a serious negotiation.” 

Marshall, who is facing a tough reelection campaign in Kansas, was critical of ICE involvement in Kansas, saying the unit “needs to coordinate with our local law enforcement.”

“Our sheriffs and police know these communities better than anyone, and working together keeps officers and residents safe,” he wrote on social platform X. 

A White House official said ICE has multiple partnerships with Kansas law enforcement.

“I don’t think that this is a particularly novel situation except that it’s Trump, and in every election candidates look for opportunities to separate themselves from their party in order to broaden their appeal,” Roe said, noting that past candidates have put distance between themselves and past presidents during elections. 

“It’s kind of normal, but Trump has not always been forgiving of people creating that separation. But I think the stakes are so high in this election that it seems to me the White House is probably a little more patient with candidates charting their own path,” he said.

data.title: New York, New Jersey declare states of emergency ahead of nor'easter
data.description:
The governors of New York, Kathy Hochul (D), and New Jersey, Mikie Sherrill (D), both announced Friday they would declare states of emergency ahead of this weekend’s nor’easter.

“I’m declaring a State of Emergency for Nassau, Suffolk, New York City and Westchester as this powerful coastal storm bears down on the region,” Hochul wrote on social media Friday afternoon. “We’re expecting dangerous coastal flooding, strong winds and potential power outages through the weekend.”

Later in the evening, Sherrill placed New Jersey’s Atlantic, Burlington, Cape May, Cumberland, Middlesex, Monmouth, Ocean and Salem counties in a state of emergency.

“I urge all New Jerseyans to take this storm seriously, stay alert, and follow local guidance. We’re prepared and will keep you updated as conditions develop,” she Sherill wrote on social media.

In Manasquan, a borough on the coast of New Jersey, officials recommended residents voluntary evacuate, according to a local NBC affiliate. The recommendations specifically targeted residents in low-lying zones, especially those who are elderly and individuals with special needs.

As the storm approaches, The Weather Channel reported wind gusts over 30 miles per hour along the coast of the Empire State and the Garden State on Friday, stretching down to parts of North Carolina. In Long Island, windspeeds reached up to 52 miles per hour.

The National Weather Service forecasted moderate to locally major flooding over the weekend, particularly in several New York City counties — prompting Mayor Zohran Mamdani to issue a statement encouraging residents to get ready for the nor’easter.

“The storm’s expected path has shifted closer to our city, bringing heavier rain and stronger winds,” Mamdani wrote.

After giving tips for how to stay safe during the storm, he concluded, “Look out for your neighbors.”
